sources.title: The Sopranos, glorious pioneer of today’s TV golden age

discussion.body: Albrecht's worry is the classic note to protect the lead's likability. The better argument is Chase's: a protagonist who refuses the ugly job when the story demands it stops being believable.
But “viewers loved it” only establishes what this audience accepted in this case. It does not make Chase's rule a general law about antiheroes.

items.title: The Sopranos: Chris Albrecht's Fear and David Chase's Blunt Reply
items.body:
HBO had already taken a gamble on The Sopranos, picking it up after every network rejected it. Its CEO, Chris Albrecht, still blanched when showrunner David Chase wanted Tony Soprano to garrotte Febby, fearing viewers would not root for a protagonist who strangled a man in cold blood.

Chase's reply was blunt: if Tony did not do it, the character would be full of shit, and therefore so would the show. He got his way, and viewers loved it.

sources.title: Replicants and robots: what can the ancient Greeks teach us?

discussion.body: Rejuvenation as full fluid replacement: out with the blood, in with the herb juice. It makes a vampire look fussy about refreshments.
The name is the tell. Medea means “to devise”, which makes her rejuvenation feel less like a miracle and more like a technique—with a very alarming bedside manner.

items.title: Medea's Rejuvenation Method: Blood Out, Herbs In
items.body:
Medea's name means “to devise”, and the myth gives her arcane arts including secrets of rejuvenation. To demonstrate her powers, she appeared to Jason and the Argonauts as a stooped old woman, then transformed herself into a beautiful young princess.

Jason fell under her spell and became her lover. He asked her to restore the youthful vigour of his aged father, Aeson. Her method was no gentle spa treatment: she drew all the blood from the old man's veins and replaced it with the juices of powerful herbs.

The myth is more than a body-horror set piece: for the ancient Greeks, the question of what it meant to be human was an obsession.

sources.title: UN says we're going to blow past 1.5º warming, offers a "now what?" answer

discussion.body: The shift from a threshold to a duration is the interesting part: a line you either stay under or cross becomes a damage-control problem with quantities you can argue about.
Those quantities are also where the optimism can hide. If the target depends on removing hundreds of gigatonnes of CO2, it is a bet on carbon removal as much as on emissions cuts.

items.title: UNEP Concedes the 1.5°C Warming Goal Is No Longer Viable
items.body:
The United Nations Environmental Programme has acknowledged, for the first time, that keeping warming below 1.5°C is no longer a viable goal.

Its replacement goalposts focus on the overshoot itself: at a minimum, limiting both how long temperatures exceed the line and by how much.

Meeting that would require dramatic emissions cuts now and the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the century is out. The current El Niño event, which appears exceptionally strong, will almost certainly push the world over that line no matter which temperature records are used.

sources.title: MPs moving to restrict gambling ads in Canada amid mounting harms

discussion.body: The study counted logos as well as other gambling messages; a logo gets a second life when a news broadcast shows highlights, so the exposure does not end with the game.
Which makes the 3,000 figure a measure of exposure, not proof that any particular message changed a bettor's behavior. It is a count, not a causal estimate.

items.title: Canada's Gambling-Ad Bill Nears a Vote; Seven Televised NHL Playoff Games Carried 3,000 Gambling Messages
items.body:
CBC reports that the federal standing committee on Canadian heritage meets next week to vote on Bill S-211, which proposes to rein in gambling advertising across the country, amid new findings of increased addiction and gambling-related suicides in Ontario.

The bill has already passed the Senate; if approved at committee, it would go to a third and final reading in the House of Commons.

For its analysis, CBC partnered with the University of Bristol to assess the 2026 NHL playoffs and count logos and gambling messages. Across seven televised games featuring Canadian teams, viewers faced 3,000 gambling messages.

sources.title: Children in care to get £10 a week savings

discussion.body: The design detail worth liking is the start date. Beginning at entry into care rather than at 16 or 18 means the balance is accumulated by the system on the child's behalf, not scraped together by a teenager who has just been handed adult bills.

The exit is the more interesting half: at 18 they can stay with the charity or move the money to an account of their own choosing. That hands a genuine decision to someone who has just turned 18, which is either trust or a very small amount of money to be trusted with.

Probably the latter. The States of Guernsey itself talks about the significant financial pressures of setting up a home and managing everyday living costs, and ten pounds a week is a gesture with excellent paperwork.

items.title: Ten Pounds a Week Set Aside for Children in Care, Collectable at 18
items.body:
A new savings scheme established by the States' children and family services department and the charity Guernsey Community Savings will set aside £10 a week for children in care, for them to access when they turn 18. The States said it applies to children from entry into the care system, and 40 will benefit immediately.

Guernsey Community Savings will open and manage the accounts, working with each young person and their social worker as they approach their 18th birthday.

sources.title: In You Can See Everything, it’s Elizabeth Holmes’s partner who makes for 2026’s timeliest villain

discussion.body: What makes the tech-bro label land, on the Guardian's account, is the template with the technology removed: paranoia, delusions of grandeur, lofty-sounding projects that never amount to anything, a seeming possessiveness toward his partner, and not even a modicum of demonstrated expertise — seemingly not even in his own imaginings.

Tech villain still feels like borrowed menace, though. The man is a not-particularly-famous partner in a four-character drama: there is no company to inspect and no product to distrust, which is somehow worse. The unsettling part is how little there is to check.

items.title: Elizabeth Holmes's Partner Demanded a Percentage of the Film's Profits
items.body:
Evans is Elizabeth Holmes's partner: she has said they are not legally married, though they got engaged in 2018 and have two children, and they seem to treat each other as spouses. He is not particularly famous, and his screen time competes with three well-known faces in what is essentially a four-character drama.

Then comes the meeting, where he demands a percentage of the film's profits — the sort of arrangement, the Guardian notes, that might be reserved for a promotional piece commissioned by a musician rather than a nonfiction film built around interviews with a notorious subject. Fielder and Oppenheim zero in on whether Holmes knew about the request and what became of it. What he gets, at least temporarily, is profit participation — which the paper casts as a violation of documentary norms.

sources.title: How long does it take to save up for a starter home? Twice as long as it did in 2019

discussion.body: The wait is only half the story; the other half is how the queue is sorted. Calhoun says cash purchases are way up, those who bought when prices were far lower have accumulated enormous equity as values climbed, and for younger buyers the overwhelming way to come up with the money, as the piece describes it, is assistance from family and friends.

Sorting by who already has family wealth explains who gets in now, not what to do about it. The report's own fix is supply — zoning and other reforms to encourage duplexes, townhomes and manufactured housing — and Congress passed a law this year aimed at that, though the onus falls on states and cities and new supply takes time.

items.title: A Median-Income Renter Household Needs 16 Years to Save a Down Payment — Twice the 2019 Wait
items.body: Mike Calhoun, president of the Center for Responsible Lending, sums up the shift: over the last seven years, the time needed to save a down payment and closing costs has doubled. The center's calculation for a median-income renter household is 16 years of saving to cover a down payment and closing costs on a starter home. That is twice as long as in 2019, and for a median-income Black renter household the estimate stretches to 21 years. The backdrop is plain enough: renters' incomes have not kept pace, and personal savings rates have dropped.

sources.title: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email

discussion.body: The reused password is the least exotic link and the most consequential: it gained an attacker access to a Tor management server, and a backdoor first discovered 12 years ago was installed.

The SSH hop is the stranger part: from the management server, the attacker connected to a second Tor server, Switzerland2, using an RSA key investigators could not find among Switzerland2's authorized keys.

items.title: More Than 300 Tor Exit Nodes Were Reconfigured to Favor Unencrypted Email
items.body:
More than 300 Tor exit nodes were hijacked and reconfigured to favor unencrypted email traffic and to route SSH connections through servers the attackers controlled, Ars Technica reports.

The takeover began in late August when, according to Tor volunteers, an attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker installed Ebury, a Linux backdoor discovered 12 years ago.

With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well and reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted.

sources.title: Kant’s Moral Philosophy

discussion.body: The interesting move is starting with what people already mean by duty and a good will, then asking what principle those judgments presuppose.

That still leaves the genuine skeptic untouched: Kant does not appear to be primarily addressing someone who doubts she has any reason to act morally at all, no matter what culture she finds herself in.

items.title: Kant Tried to State the Principle Behind Ordinary Moral Judgments
items.body:
Kant proceeds by analyzing and elucidating commonsense ideas about morality, including the ideas of a good will and duty. The point is to arrive at a precise statement of the principle on which all ordinary moral judgments are based.

Those judgments are supposed to be ones any normal, sane, adult human being would accept, at least on due rational reflection. Many would now regard Kant as overly optimistic about the depth and extent of moral agreement. Perhaps he is best thought of as drawing on a moral viewpoint that is very widely shared and contains some general judgments that are very deeply held.

sources.title: How ‘Goodfellas’ Serves As the Bridge Between ‘The Godfather’ and ‘The Sopranos’

discussion.body: The essay's observation that any conversation about Goodfellas inevitably involves The Godfather or The Sopranos is really a point about canon formation: some works arrive with their context attached.

Influence is not the same as quality, though. The essay notes Roger Ebert thought Goodfellas was better than The Godfather and David Chase acknowledges it inspired The Sopranos; neither settles the ranking.

items.title: The Ringer's Case That Goodfellas Is the Hardest of the Mob Trilogy to Discuss Alone
items.body:
Goodfellas opened on September 19, 1990—between the March 1972 release of The Godfather and the January 1999 premiere of The Sopranos. The essay's frame is an informal American mob trilogy, and within that frame it calls Goodfellas the hardest to talk about on its own—and says it might be the greatest artistic achievement of the three.

The essay says Goodfellas's importance is harder to quantify, in part because The Godfather revolutionized the movies and The Sopranos revolutionized TV.

sources.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

discussion.body: The appealing part is the order of operations: authenticate the human before the model gets to plan. It treats the prompt as something that arrives with a principal attached.
A valid JWT establishes who the caller is, but not what they can see. The walkthrough's query layer, Denodo VDP, is where access policies evaluate.

items.title: Before the Model Plans a Query, the Gateway Checks the Human's JWT
items.body:
In an AWS Machine Learning walkthrough, the inbound path starts before the model: a client sends the user's request through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates a JSON Web Token identifying the human user against the enterprise identity provider, then routes the request to the AgentCore runtime that hosts the Strands agent. The agent then invokes a foundation model on Bedrock—Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 in the walkthrough—to interpret the prompt and plan the query.

AWS describes AgentCore as a platform to build, connect and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. That matters for agentic systems that need governed access to live enterprise data: the gateway can establish the human principal while the runtime hosts the agent and the model plans the query.

sources.title: Dehydration, UTIs and cognitive health: Getting enough to drink is complicated for people with brain disorders

discussion.body: The Ontario figure is a useful rebuke to the idea that dehydration is just a failure of personal discipline. In long-term care, one in six residents is an operational problem, not a character flaw.

True, but that number belongs specifically to long-term care residents aged 65 and older. It would be a mistake to stretch it into a claim about every older adult with dementia; the narrower point is that some people need help acting on the advice.

items.title: About One in Six Ontario Long-Term Care Residents Aged 65+ Experienced Dehydration in a Study. 'Drink More Water' Is Not Always Enough.
items.body:
About one in six Ontario long-term care residents aged 65 and older experienced dehydration during the study period, according to a study of more than 96,000 residents. For older adults with dementia or Parkinson's disease, staying hydrated can be more complicated than simply drinking more water. People with brain disorders, including dementia and Parkinson's, may need help putting that advice into action.

UTIs are more common among older adults yet are often missed because symptoms are atypical. Sudden unexplained confusion or changes in alertness or behaviour are reasons to seek prompt medical assessment.

sources.title: Smoke Gets in Your Eyes: Animal Sacrifice and the Greek Gods

discussion.body: The raw cuts are the best detail because they make the gods seem like inspectors: the meat has to prove where it came from.
Cute, but the more serious point is that sacrifice served to separate gods and human beings and to define who is who.

items.title: The Gods Got Bones and Fat; the Worshippers Got the Meat
items.body:
Ancient Greeks—and others in the ancient eastern Mediterranean—sacrificed animals to their gods, rendering the animals to meat offered to the gods and to the worshippers themselves. A typical offering was a thigh bone from cattle, sheep, goats or pigs, wrapped in fat and set ablaze; the worshippers got the rest. The gods, in other words, got smoke and bones, while the humans got dinner.

The ritual was not only a meal transaction. Animal sacrifice served to separate gods and human beings and to define who is who. In other rituals, choice cuts were left raw for the gods, a display that proved to the gods where the meat originated. That is a strange and vivid idea: the offering is also evidence of provenance.

sources.title: A GOP congressman voted to cut Medicaid. It covers 62% of his district. Can he win?

discussion.body: Six in ten is not an abstraction; it is the electorate. A Medicaid vote in a district like that is a household vote.
Valadao's 'no actual cuts' may be a budget-baseline argument, but it is a hard sell where six in ten are enrolled.
The sharper issue is timing: eligibility checks that start after the midterms are where coverage actually gets tested.

items.title: Six in Ten Constituents on Medicaid, and Valadao's 'No Actual Cuts'
items.body:
In this Central Valley toss-up district, roughly six in ten constituents are enrolled in Medicaid. Challenger Randy Villegas, a political science professor, has embraced 'Medicare for All' and says Valadao's vote 'is going to rip away healthcare from Valley families.'

The attack has a specific mechanism: many working-age adults may not satisfy new work requirements and twice-a-year eligibility checks that, NPR says, start after the midterm elections by political design. Valadao, in a televised Oct. 6 debate, said 'there are no actual cuts' to Medicaid.

sources.title: Simone de Beauvoir

discussion.body: The vow is the quotable part; the friendship is the more interesting defiance. Two schoolgirls against a whole code of femininity is a better scene than a lone rebel.
Then Zaza dies in 1929, and the resistance story ends in heartbreak rather than a manifesto.
The father detail complicates the rebellion: the encouragement to write came from a man whose intelligence she admired, even as she rebelled against bourgeois ideology.

items.title: Beauvoir's Girlhood Vow and the Schoolfriend Who Resisted With Her
items.body:
Simone de Beauvoir was born in Paris in 1908. As a child she vowed never to become a housewife or mother, and she admired her father's intelligence. He introduced her to great works of literature and encouraged her to write.

At school she formed an intimate bond with Elizabeth Mabille, or Zaza, and together they confronted and resisted the rigid expectations of bourgeois, Catholic femininity. Beauvoir spent much of her childhood rebelling against the values of her faith and bourgeois ideology. When Zaza died of meningitis in 1929, Beauvoir suffered intense heartbreak.

sources.title: Indonesia Drafts New Film Law as Jakarta, Home to Four Netflix Productions, Courts International Shoots (EXCLUSIVE)

discussion.body: The incentives are tangible—50% off certain location fees and a 50% admissions tax concession for qualifying Indonesian films—while the law has no parliamentary date.
No date is not the same as no movement. The film agency chair says the first draft has taken shape since Cannes and that the direction is right, though he is not ready to say more.

items.title: Jakarta Offers Film Incentives While the Revised Film Law Waits
items.body:
Indonesia's film agency is helping draft a revised Film Law that would reshape its powers, while Jakarta works to become a regional film hub.

The Jakarta Film Commission launched in June alongside Filming in Jakarta, a one-stop service for producers.

Jakarta has cut certain location fees by 50% and introduced a 50% tax concession on cinema admissions for qualifying Indonesian films.

sources.title: Politics is widening U.S. gender divides. In Canada? It's complicated

discussion.body: The useful part is the mechanism: Parkin treats the U.S. reaction as a response to a specific political figure, not as an automatic stage of modern life.

That mechanism is about a broad pattern, but the campus reporting shows the subject is hardly absent: most University of Ottawa students CBC spoke with either called politics pivotal in relationships or said they avoid bringing it up altogether.

items.title: North of the Border, the Youth Gender-Political Split Looks Different
items.body:
Andrew Parkin, executive director of the Environics Institute for Survey Research, tells CBC that young people aren't feeling the same political split north of the border.

Parkin says people in the U.S. are reacting to their political developments, and that 'we haven't had a leader like Trump to provoke that kind of reaction.'

He also says men are not generally becoming more conservative.

sources.title: Some New Yorkers back ban on horse-drawn carriages, but drivers fear for incomes

discussion.body: The seven-incident figure is the strongest pro-ban fact, but it arrives from a group that supports the ban and uses the broad label 'horse-related'.
The broad label doesn't make the drivers' no-risk claim convincing. In May, a spooked horse hit another carriage, tipped it over, and sent a driver to hospital.

items.title: Central Park Carriage Drivers Say the Rides Are Safe. The Conservancy Counts Seven Incidents in 13 Months.
items.body:
The city is moving this week to outlaw horse-drawn carriages over animal and public-safety concerns. Several Central Park carriage drivers who spoke to the BBC said they were devoted to their horses and that the rides did not pose a safety risk. Medet Fidan, a carriage driver for 12 years, called allegations of mistreatment a joke.

The Central Park Conservancy, the non-profit organisation that manages Central Park and supports the ban, said that over the past 13 months alone there had been seven 'horse-related incidents'.

sources.title: How Do We Know That Epic Poems Were Recited from Memory?

discussion.body: The aluminum disks are the satisfying part. Parry had textual analysis and anthropology to draw on, but the field work left actual recordings of guslari performing epic songs — the argument arrives with sound on it.

What those recordings establish is that pre-literate people could recite long poems. Whether the Iliad and the Odyssey were in fact carried that way before being written down stays a possibility — the fantastical notion made plausible, not a documented history of those two poems.

items.title: Parry Took Aluminum Disks to Bosnia to Record Guslari Performing Epic Songs
items.body:
The idea that long, involved poems like the Iliad and the Odyssey might have been recited by pre-literate peoples before being committed to writing once struck scholars as too fantastical to take seriously.

Parry used textual analysis, anthropology and field work to show that pre-literate or semi-literate peoples could, in fact, recite long poems. Inspired by the Slavicist Matija Murko, who attended his thesis defense at the Sorbonne, Parry headed to the hills of what is now called Bosnia in the early 1930s. There he used aluminum disks to record pre-literate bards, guslari, performing epske pjesme, epic oral songs — not reconstructing the feat from theory but capturing it as it was done.

sources.title: Why romantic relationships matter more to men than to women

discussion.body: The self-sufficient man has had centuries of good press. Against the essay's premise that love carries disproportionate weight for men, that pose starts to look less like a description of how men thrive than a story they tell about themselves.

Careful with the shape of it, though. The 46 per cent is a comparison of mortality risk between unmarried and married men across millions of records — a difference between groups, not a demonstration that the relationship itself is what keeps anyone alive. It reads better as a puzzle than a prescription.

items.title: Unmarried Men's Mortality Risk Was 46% Higher Than Married Men's, a 2020 Meta-Analysis Found
items.body:
A 2020 meta-analysis by Yafeng Wang of Wuhan University and colleagues pooled data on marital status and mortality risk covering 7.9 million individuals and 1.9 million deaths. It found unmarried women had a 22 per cent higher mortality risk than married women — and unmarried men had a 46 per cent higher risk than married men.

Set that against the older picture of the self-sufficient man who shuns romance as a noble figure. Francis Bacon, in “Of Marriage and the Single Life” (1625), wrote that a man with wife and children “hath given hostages to fortune”; Psyche's essay reads him as treating romance and family as impediments to a man becoming his best. Which makes the mortality figures a strange advertisement for the lone-wolf ideal: the state the tradition praised as freedom is the one associated with the shorter life.
